content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching the cedar—especially the cedar of Lebanon—primarily symbolizes strength, majesty, and enduring stature, applied most often to the flourishing and stability of the righteous person who is planted and grows under God's blessing. The tree's great height, longevity, deep rooting, and incorruptible fragrant wood make it the standard biblical image of noble, God-given greatness.","primary_basis":["Psalm 92:12 – 'The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon'","Psalm 104:16 – 'The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted'","Song of Solomon 5:15 – the beloved's countenance 'excellent as the cedars,' read as majesty/beauty","Psalm 29:5 – the voice of the LORD breaking the cedars, presupposing them as the epitome of strength","1 Kings 5–7 and 6:9–20 – cedar as the choice material for Solomon's temple, connoting durability, purity, and worthiness for God's dwelling","2 Samuel 7:2,7 – a 'house of cedar' as the mark of royal dignity"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Human pride, loftiness, and worldly power destined for divine judgment—the cedar as the tall thing God brings low (applied to Assyria, Lebanon, and the arrogant generally).","basis":["Isaiah 2:12–13 – the day of the LORD 'upon all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up'","Ezekiel 31:3–14 – Assyria as a towering cedar cut down","Isaiah 10:33–34; Zechariah 11:1–2 – felling of cedars as judgment on the proud","Amos 2:9 – the Amorite 'whose height was like the height of the cedars,' destroyed"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Royal-Davidic and messianic symbolism: the cedar sprig planted by God as the restored Davidic kingdom or the Messiah, under whose branches all find shelter; often connected typologically to kingdom parables.","basis":["Ezekiel 17:3–4, 22–24 – God takes a tender twig from the high cedar and plants it on Israel's mountain","2 Samuel 7 – 'house of cedar' motif in the Davidic covenant context","Frequently linked by commentators to the mustard-seed/tree imagery of Matthew 13:31–32"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Purification, incorruptibility, and (in patristic/typological reading) the incorruptible humanity of Christ or the wood of the cross; cedar's use in cleansing rites and its rot-resistant wood ground this reading.","basis":["Leviticus 14:4–6, 49–52 – cedar wood in the cleansing of lepers and houses","Numbers 19:6 – cedar wood burned with the red heifer","Patristic and medieval typology (e.g., traditions that the cross included cedar; allegorical readings of temple cedar as Christ's flesh)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The Church, the saints, or spiritual growth in holiness—an ecclesial-allegorical extension of Psalm 92:12 and the temple imagery, common in devotional and homiletical literature.","basis":["Psalm 92:12–14 – planted in the house of the LORD, flourishing in God's courts","1 Kings 6 – cedar-lined temple allegorized as the Church/believer as God's dwelling","Hosea 14:5–6 – Israel's restored growth 'as Lebanon'"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"Cedar is a genuinely bivalent biblical symbol: the same qualities (height, grandeur) signify righteous flourishing and divine blessing in the Psalms and temple texts, but pride ripe for judgment in the prophets. The 'strength/majesty/flourishing of the righteous' sense is the one most commonly presented as primary in Christian teaching, dictionaries of biblical imagery, and homiletics, with the pride-and-judgment reading widely acknowledged as the prophetic counterpoint rather than a rival definition. Reference works (e.g., Dictionary of Biblical Imagery–type sources) typically list both, with Psalm 92:12 as the anchor text. No single verse defines cedar symbolism; the consensus rests on the cumulative pattern across roughly 70 Old Testament occurrences."}
